idiom_name: state as fields of the smallest owning struct; per-request values in handler locals and captured closures; package-level vars reserved for process-wide configuration
implementation_notes: Go's scope rules make the placement decision concrete: declare the state as a field of the struct that owns the behaviour (one component or handler type per struct), keep per-request and per-interaction values in the handler's locals or in a closure that captures them, and reserve package-level variables for process-wide configuration or genuinely shared state. The replacement for the classic structure is exactly that struct ownership: a component carries its own state and methods, instead of sharing one package-level record every function reads. When two components must observe the same value, put it in the smallest struct both can reach (or pass it explicitly through the call chain) rather than promoting it to the package; and when the value is shared across goroutines, the owner struct is also the natural home for the mutex that guards it.
pitfalls: A package-level var is process-wide state shared by every importer; using one for per-request or per-user values is the Go shape of over-lifted state and races under concurrency.

State shared between goroutines needs synchronization in its owner (a mutex field next to the state, or a channel); a bare struct field written from several goroutines is a data race even though it lives in one struct.
Closures keep captured variables alive, so a captured pointer or a handler registered on a long-lived registry can pin state and its allocation far longer than the interaction that created it.
